content: CD99, also referred to as MIC2 or single-chain type-1 glycoprotein, is a highly O-glycosylated transmembrane protein encoded by the CD99 gene in humans. This protein has a molecular weight of 32 kDa. Uniquely, despite being located on the X chromosome, the CD99 gene does not undergo X inactivation. It was the first pseudoautosomal gene discovered in humans. CD99 is expressed on all leukocytes, with the highest levels observed on thymocytes. It is believed to enhance T-cell adhesion and promote apoptosis in double-positive T cells. Additionally, CD99 is found in endothelial cells and within the periodontium, including gingival fibroblasts and gingival epithelial cells. It plays a role in cell migration and activation. Experimental evidence suggests that CD99 binds to cyclophilin A. This protein is present on the cell surface of Ewing's sarcoma tumors and is also expressed in granulosa cell tumors. In malignant gliomas, CD99 expression is higher compared to normal brain tissue, and this overexpression is associated with increased invasiveness and reduced survival rates. Antibodies targeting CD99 are utilized in diagnostic immunohistochemistry to differentiate Ewing's sarcoma from other tumors with similar histological features. They are also used to identify thymic tumors and spindle cell tumors, such as synovial sarcoma, haemangiopericytoma, and meningioma. The EWS/FLI fusion protein is thought to regulate CD99 expression, but knocking down EWS/FLI only modestly reduces CD99 levels. When CD99 expression is knocked down in human Ewing's sarcoma cells and these cells are grafted into mice, the development of tumors and bone metastases is significantly reduced. Reduced CD99 expression leads to increased β-III tubulin expression and enhanced neurite outgrowth. Conversely, upregulating CD99 expression in the L428 cell line, a Hodgkin's lymphoma cell line, induces redifferentiation of these cells toward B cells. This suggests that the loss of B-cell differentiation in Hodgkin's lymphoma may be linked to CD99 downregulation. Interestingly, men appear to express higher levels of CD99 than women. In terms of prognostic value, in patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the germinal center B-cell (GCB) subtype, positive CD99 expression is associated with improved 2-year event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS) compared to negative CD99 expression. However, in patients with non-GCB DLBCL, negative CD99 expression correlates with better 2-year EFS and OS. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), higher CD99 expression in the stromal tissue is linked to a more favorable prognosis. Regarding its interactions, CD99 has been shown to inhibit cell-extracellular matrix adhesion by suppressing β1 integrin affinity.
